evidence.note: Claim CONFIRMED: a new [section] is addable as a single new config_sections file (its own @declare) with NO edit to config/_core.py field list or config/__init__.py re-export list. Mechanism: @declare records SECTION_CLASSES[name]=cls in _docs.py; Config injects its section fields from that registry via _SectionFields.__init_subclass__ (sorted); ddflow.config re-exports *Config lazily via module __getattr__. Refuting observation before fix: _core.py hand-listed 53 fields and __init__.py re-listed 53 classes. Cheapest test: tests/test_config_layout.py::test_a_section_is_wired_from_declare_not_a_kept_list - fails on unfixed (SECTION_CLASSES absent) and asserts _section_types()==SECTION_CLASSES plus each class re-exported. Ran: uv run pytest tests/test_config_layout.py -q -> 9 passed.

chunk_findings.detail: The dynamic section fields are added after the `Config` class body has already placed `sources` in `cls.__annotations__`, and the loop uses `sorted(SECTION_CLASSES)` instead of the registry order promised by the class docstring. As a result the generated dataclass field order is `sources` first and the sections alphabetically, whereas the removed explicit `Config` had `lease, worktree, ..., sources` last. This silently changes the positional `__init__` parameter order and `dataclasses.asdict(Config())` key order; for example, an old positional call `Config(LeaseConfig(...))` would now bind that object to `sources` rather than `lease`, silently corrupting the config object.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: `Config` is assembled from `SECTION_CLASSES` at class-creation time, but this hunk never imports that name and never imports section modules. `SECTION_CLASSES` is a new symbol in `_docs.py`, and the only `_core.py` hunk does not bind it, so defining `Config` raises `NameError` on `sorted(SECTION_CLASSES)`. Even after an import is added, `declare()` only fills the dict when each section module is imported; `SECTION_NAMES` is `pkgutil` discovery and does not import them, and the old per-class names in this file are now unused so they no longer have to be imported. A new `config_sections/notify.py` with `@declare("notify")` therefore never becomes a field: after `from ddflow.config._core import Config`, `Config().notify` raises `AttributeError`. The hub edit is not removed; it is either still required as an import or the section is silently dropped. The same hook also appends fields after the class body, so `sources` is the first dataclass field, not last: `Config(lease_value)` now assigns that value to `sources` and leaves `lease` at the default, and field order is not `SECTION_NAMES` as the comment in `config_sections/__init__.py` claims.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression never checks that `Config` fields are assembled from the section registry instead of a hand-written hub list. Given code that still declares every section as a field on `Config` in `ddflow/config/_core.py` (the lease this bug is about) and also exports `SECTION_CLASSES` equal to `_section_types()`, both assertions pass: `_section_types() == dict(SECTION_CLASSES)` only compares two type maps, and `getattr(C, cls.__name__)` only checks the package re-export. The docstring even says the unfixed failure was an import of `SECTION_CLASSES`, not a failed assertion on `Config`, so restoring the one-line hub edit does not fail this test.

chunk_findings.detail: `from ddflow.config import *` no longer binds the section classes. The previous code put `AgentConfig`, `ApprovalsConfig`, etc. in `ddflow.config.__dict__` via the `from ._core import (...)` statement, so star import (no `__all__` is defined) reused them. Module-level `__getattr__` is not consulted by star import, and the new section names are not in the module namespace, so a consumer doing `from ddflow.config import *` followed by `AgentConfig` gets a `NameError`. This is a silent regression for any caller relying on the documented re-export.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/__init__.py:__getattr__

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 1 is only partially fixed. The triage notes the fix now prepends sections so `fields(Config)` **still leads with sorted sections**, and the loop still uses `sorted(SECTION_CLASSES)` rather than the declaration/registry order. That leaves the concrete API change from the original finding: the removed explicit `Config` had `lease, worktree` as the first positional fields and `sources` last, whereas the generated order now begins with `agent` and places `lease` after `lanes`. A positional `Config(old_lease, old_worktree, ...)` is now interpreted as `agent, approvals, ...`, and `dataclasses.asdict(Config)` also emits a different field order. The fix only moved sections before bookkeeping; it did not restore the promised registry/old positional order.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: `dict(sorted(SECTION_CLASSES.items()))` still sorts section names alphabetically, not “in the registry’s order” promised by the `_SectionFields` docstring. The removed explicit `Config` started with `lease, worktree, flow, ...`; the generated dataclass now starts with the alphabetically first entries (`agent, approvals, bugs, ...`), so any positional `Config(lease_config, worktree_config, ...)` call silently assigns those objects to the wrong fields, and `dataclasses.fields(Config)` / `dataclasses.asdict` output is reordered. Either the docstring must say alphabetical, or the `sorted()` must be removed to honor registry order.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: Because `__init_subclass__` is inherited by subclasses of `Config`, a `@dataclass class MyConfig(Config): extra: int = 0` triggers the injection a second time on `MyConfig`, re-adding every section name to `MyConfig.__annotations__` and `MyConfig.__dict__`. The `@dataclass` decorator then treats these as attempts to overwrite the existing `Config` dataclass fields and raises `TypeError` on the first section field. The old hard-coded `Config` dataclass accepted such a subclass. The hook should avoid re-injecting for subclasses of `Config`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: The regression only scans `CONFIG_DIR / "_core.py"` for a hand-kept per-section dataclass field. It never scans `ddflow/config/__init__.py` for a hand-kept per-section re-export, even though the docstring explicitly names that file and the bug is about both hub files. A concrete false green: re-add `LeaseConfig = _core.LeaseConfig` (or `from ._core import LeaseConfig`) in `config/__init__.py`; `_section_types() == dict(SECTION_CLASSES)` still holds, `getattr(C, "LeaseConfig") is LeaseConfig` still returns the same class via the explicit export, and the `_core.py` regex passes, so the test passes while the `config/__init__.py` half of B-config-section-needs-hub-edit has recurred.

chunk_findings.detail: The method does `sections = dict(sorted(SECTION_CLASSES.items()))`, so it discards the registry's insertion order, even though the class docstring promises fields are added "in the registry's order." The removed explicit list was not alphabetical (`lease`, `worktree`, `flow`, ...), but the replacement alphabetizes the dataclass fields. For example, under a non-alphabetical `SECTION_CLASSES` registry, `dataclasses.fields(Config)[0].name` changes from `"lease"` to `"agent"`. A positional call written for the previous generated `__init__`, such as `Config(lease, worktree, flow)`, silently binds the first argument to `agent` instead of `lease`; dataclasses do not type-check, so this produces a misconfigured Config rather than an error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: `__init_subclass__` is inherited by every subclass of `Config`, not just run once for `Config` itself. A caller who defines `@dataclass class MyConfig(Config): extra: int = 0` triggers the hook on `MyConfig`: it prepends all `SECTION_CLASSES` names to `MyConfig.__annotations__` and assigns a `field(...)` for each. `@dataclass` then sees every section name as both an inherited Config field and a subclass annotation, and raises `TypeError: Cannot overwrite attribute '<first-section>'`. This makes Config un-subclassable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_section_is_wired_from_declare_not_a_kept_list` imports `_section_types` from `tests.test_config_layout` (or expects it to be defined in scope), but `_section_types` is not defined anywhere in `tests/test_config_layout.py` or imported from another module in the provided diff, causing a `NameError` when executing `assert _section_types() == dict(SECTION_CLASSES)`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_config_layout.py:116

chunk_findings.detail: `__init_subclass__` injects every `SECTION_CLASSES` name into the subclass annotations and class dict. `@dataclass` then treats those as fields declared on the subclass as well as inherited from `Config`. Input: `@dataclass\nclass Child(Config):\n    extra: int = 1` (or even a dataclass subclass with no new fields) raises `TypeError: <section> is a field in class Child, but it is already a field in base class Config`. An undecorated subclass still gets the section `Field`s setattr onto it, shadowing the base fields. The hook should run only when `Config` itself is created, not for every further subclass.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config/_core.py:_SectionFields.__init_subclass__

data.probe: Refuted: `from ddflow.config import *` does NOT raise ImportError here. CPythons star-import iterates __all__ and calls getattr(module, name) for each, which triggers the module __getattr__ (PEP 562), so a name resolved lazily via __getattr__ still binds. Empirically verified: exec("from ddflow.config import *") binds AgentConfig to ddflow.config_sections.agent.AgentConfig and LeaseConfig (printed __name__). The reviewer misread the PEP 562 star-import interaction.
